query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray distance in the HVAF-i7 process to increase in-flight particle velocity will improve the deposition efficiency and enable the formation of a thicker, high-integrity FeCoNiCrAl bond coat.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder in the 15–45 μm size range, which under standard HVAF-i7 conditions yields coatings with acceptable adhesion and low as-sprayed oxidation but insufficient thickness.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 process by reducing the spray (nozzle-to-substrate) distance (targeting the lower end of the 300–350 mm range) to increase the particle velocity.
generation.conditions: Deposition performed on substrates including internal diameters as small as 120 mm and under conditions representative of high-temperature thermal-barrier service.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased in-flight particle kinetic energy enhances particle deformation upon impact, leading to better bonding and accumulation of material.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the spray distance, the particles gain higher velocity, which improves the momentum transfer at impact. The enhanced kinetic energy promotes superior splat formation and bonding, resulting in higher deposition efficiency and thicker coatings without a significant penalty on in-spray oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HVAF-i7 process will yield a coating with a significantly increased thickness compared to the baseline, while maintaining acceptable levels of oxidation resistance and adhesion.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced with standard HVAF-i7 settings using 15–45 μm feedstock that provide acceptable quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective as long as the reduced spray distance does not induce excessive substrate heating or excessive in-flight oxidation that could compromise the microstructural integrity and adhesion of the coating.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the balance between increased particle velocity and the potential risk of inducing local overheating or oxidation; optimization may be needed to prevent any deleterious effects on the coating microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled experiment comparing two sets of HVAF-i7 depositions on substrates with internal diameters of ~120 mm. The control group will use standard spray distance parameters while the experimental group will use a reduced spray distance (targeting 300–350 mm) to increase particle velocity. All other parameters and the 15–45 μm feedstock will be held constant.
measurements: Coating thickness via cross-sectional microscopy (SEM) to assess deposition efficiency.
Adhesion tests (e.g., pull-off tests) to evaluate bonding strength.
Oxidation assessment using XRD and EDS to quantify as-sprayed oxidation levels.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced spray distance does not result in a statistically significant increase in coating thickness compared to the control or if it causes a significant degradation in oxidation resistance or adhesion, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

As reported in [,,,], HVOF as-sprayed AlTiCrFeCoNi coatings possessed a dense microstructure and a high microhardness over 750 HV with a good fracture toughness. The heat-treated NiCoFeCrSiAlTi coating exhibits a hardness even higher than 800 HV, good wear resistance, and oxidation resistance at 1100 °C, similar to that of MCrAlY coating []. The cavitation erosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi coating is about 3.5 times that of 06Cr13Ni5Mo steel in the same environment []. The high wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA at elevated temperatures is associated with oxidation behavior. The formation of a compact oxide layer on the AlCoCrFeNi and AlTiCrFeCoNi HVOF coatings accounts for enhanced wear resistance at temperatures ≥ 800 °C [] and a lowered coefficient of friction due to its function as a solid lubricant []. In [], it was found that additions of Nd and Mo to a AlCrFeCoNi base significantly reduced the wear depth at increasing temperatures due to improved oxide layer adhesion. Thus, AlCoCrFeNiMo coatings deposited using HVOF are suitable for high-temperature application. drafts.hypothesis: Increasing the in‐flight particle velocity by optimizing the nozzle-to-substrate distance (targeting ~300–350 mm) during the HVAF-i7 process will overcome the thickness limitation for FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy coatings.
drafts.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder (15–45 μm) deposited by HVAF‐i7, which currently yields acceptable coating quality but insufficient thickness.
drafts.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 process to increase particle velocity—specifically, by reducing the standoff distance (to around 300–350 mm) and/or increasing fuel/oxygen flow to boost particle acceleration.
drafts.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch under conditions typical for bond-coat applications, including deposition within confined internal diameters (as small as 120 mm) and service under high-temperature thermal-barrier conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic energy of particles leads to better in-flight deformation, improved splat formation and bonding upon impact, resulting in higher deposition efficiency and thicker coatings without significantly increasing as-sprayed oxidation.
drafts.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases the impact energy on the substrate, which promotes better flattening and bond formation. This improved in-flight kinetic energy allows more material to be retained on the substrate per pass, effectively increasing coating thickness while maintaining the desirable microstructural integrity and oxidation control.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under the modified HVAF-i7 conditions the resulting bond coat will achieve a significantly increased thickness relative to the current state, with deposition efficiency and integrity comparable to that obtained using the HVAF-M3 system, while still retaining low in-spray oxidation and high durability at elevated service temperatures.
drafts.baseline: Using the standard HVAF-i7 parameters with 15–45 μm feedstock yields acceptable microstructure and adhesion but inadequate thickness compared to M3 system results.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective provided that the optimized standoff distance and increased particle velocity do not induce excessive in-flight oxidation or compromise coating adhesion. Its success is limited to the specific powder size (15–45 μm) and will need to be validated within the geometric constraints (internal diameters as small as 120 mm) of the intended substrates.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study using the HVAF-i7 system with two sets of parameters: one using the standard spray distance and fuel settings (control) and another using the reduced standoff distance (300–350 mm) and adjusted fuel/oxygen parameters to increase particle velocity. Keep the feedstock (15–45 μm FeCoNiCrAl powder) constant. Deposit coatings on substrates with internal diameters of ~120 mm.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized HVAF-i7 conditions do not result in a statistically significant increase in coating thickness and deposition efficiency, or if the improvements negatively affect oxidation resistance or adhesion compared to the control, then the hypothesis that increased particle velocity overcomes the thickness limitation will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Increasing the particle velocity during HVAF-i7 spraying will improve the deposition efficiency enough to overcome the current thickness limitation while preserving low as‐sprayed oxidation and good adhesion.
drafts.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized FeCoNiCrAl alloy powder in the 15–45 μm range, which has been shown to yield acceptable quality coatings but with inadequate thickness on HVAF-i7.
drafts.intervention: Adjust the HVAF–i7 torch settings to generate a higher particle velocity (for example, via a modified fuel/oxygen ratio or altered combustion/nozzle configuration).
drafts.conditions: Deposition performed with similar stand-off distances (around 300–350 mm as optimal for conventional MCrAlY bond coats), on substrates including small internal diameters (~120 mm), under conditions that simulate high‐temperature thermal barrier service.
drafts.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy at impact promotes improved flattening, bonding, and material accumulation, reducing in-flight oxidation through shorter residence times.
drafts.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases momentum transfer to the substrate and improves the deposition efficiency per pass by facilitating better particle deformation and adhesion, leading to thicker coatings while keeping oxidation minimal.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified HVAF-i7 process will yield a significantly thicker, adherent bond coat compared to the baseline deposition using the standard settings, without compromising the coating integrity or oxidation resistance.
drafts.baseline: Coatings produced using the standard HVAF-i7 settings with 15–45 μm feedstock, which, although of acceptable quality, are too thin for the intended bond-coat application.
drafts.boundary: The approach should be effective under conditions typical for bond-coat service (i.e., high temperature, thermal cycling, and deposition on substrates with internal diameters down to 120 mm) without inducing excessive oxidation or compromising adhesion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings on identical substrates using the HVAF-i7 system – one with standard particle velocity settings and one with increased particle velocity (achieved by adjusting fuel/oxygen ratios or nozzle geometry) at the same optimal spray distance (300–350 mm). Deposit coatings on substrates with internal diameters down to 120 mm under simulated high-temperature service conditions.
measurements: Coating thickness measured by cross-sectional SEM.
Oxidation state assessment via XRD/EDS analysis to check for excessive in-flight oxidation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased particle velocity does not result in a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (i.e., the deposition rate remains similar to the baseline) or if the improvement comes at the expense of increased oxidation or reduced adhesion, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
